unit.title: Draw and interpret sketches and simple drawings

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a working drawing?
options: To show the customer what colour the job will be painted
To give all the information needed to make the part
To record how many hours each worker spent on the job
To show the price of the materials and the labour

questions.stem: Where on a drawing would you normally find the scale, the drawing number and the date?
options: In the parts list
Along the top edge
In the dimension lines
In the title block

questions.stem: Two copies of the same drawing have different revision letters, B and C. Which one should you work from?
options: Revision B, because it was issued first
Whichever copy is cleaner and easier to read
Revision C, because it is the latest
Either one, because they show the same part

questions.stem: A drawing is drawn to a scale of 1:2. What does this mean?
options: The drawing is half the real size
The drawing is twice the real size
Every size must be divided by 2 before cutting
The drawing shows 2 views of the part

questions.stem: On a drawing at a scale of 1:5, a line measures 40 mm. What is the real length?
options: 8 mm
45 mm
200 mm
400 mm

questions.stem: A building plan is drawn at 1:50. A wall measures 80 mm on the plan. How long is the real wall?
options: 4 m

questions.stem: Why should you work from the sizes written on a drawing, instead of measuring the drawing with a rule?
options: Copies can shrink or stretch, so measured sizes may be wrong
Measuring a drawing with a rule is slower than reading it
The steel rule might mark, crease or tear the paper drawing
Drawings are always drawn at full size anyway

questions.stem: On an engineering drawing, what does a thin dashed line usually show?
options: The centre of a hole
A dimension line
The visible outline
An edge that is hidden

questions.stem: A chain line is made of long dashes with a dot or short dash between them. Which line is used for the centre line of a hole?
options: A thick continuous line
A thin chain line
A thin dashed line
A thin wavy line

questions.stem: Which line is used to show the visible outline of a part?
options: A thick continuous line
A thin chain line
A thin dashed line
A thin continuous line with arrows

questions.stem: In an orthographic drawing, what does the plan view show?
options: The part as seen from the front
The part as seen from the side
The part cut in half
The part as seen from above

questions.stem: Why does an orthographic drawing usually show more than one view?
options: So that the drawing fills the whole sheet of paper
So that different workers can each have a view
Because one view cannot show every size and shape
Because each view is drawn at a different scale

questions.stem: In first angle projection, where is the plan view placed?
options: Below the front view
Above the front view
To the left of the front view
Beside the title block

questions.stem: How can you tell whether a drawing uses first angle or third angle projection?
options: By the colour of the lines used for the outline of the part
By the projection symbol, usually in the title block
By counting how many views there are on the sheet
By the size of the sheet the drawing is printed on

questions.stem: In an isometric drawing of a box, the horizontal edges are drawn at what angle to the horizontal?
What is the main advantage of an isometric sketch?
options: It shows every hidden detail clearly
It needs no measurements or sizes at all
It shows the part in 3D so it is easy to picture
It is the only drawing a workshop can use

questions.stem: In an oblique drawing, how is the front face of the object drawn?
options: Tilted at 30° to the horizontal
As its true shape, seen straight on
As it is seen from directly above
As a cut through the middle

questions.stem: A dimension reads 100 ± 0.5. Which measured size is acceptable?
Sizes on most engineering drawings are in millimetres. How is this usually shown?
options: A note such as "All dimensions in mm" is given once
The letters mm are written after every single number
The sizes are all written in red ink
The units are left for the worker to decide

questions.stem: Why is it good practice to give all sizes from one datum (base line) on a drawing?
options: It makes the drawing look neater
It uses fewer numbers on the drawing
Errors do not build up from one size to the next
It lets the worker choose any starting point

questions.stem: A drawing shows a note: 4 × Ø10. What does this mean?
options: One hole, 40 mm in diameter
One hole, 4 mm wide and 10 mm deep
Ten holes, each 4 mm in diameter
Four holes, each 10 mm in diameter

questions.stem: On a drawing, what does R15 mean?
options: A diameter of 15 mm
A radius of 15 mm
Revision 15 of the drawing
A run of 15 metres

questions.stem: What does NTS mean on a sketch or drawing?
options: Not to scale
Notes to supervisor
Number of total sheets
New technical standard

questions.stem: A drawing says "6 holes equally spaced on 100 PCD". What does PCD stand for?
options: Part centre distance
Plate cutting depth
Pitch circle diameter
Punch centre dot

questions.stem: On a sectional view, what do the thin lines drawn at 45° across the cut surface show?
options: Where the part has been cut through
Where the part must be painted
Where the part is to be welded
Where the part has hidden holes

questions.stem: A drawing of a steel gate has a parts list (bill of materials). What does it tell you?
options: The name and job title of each worker who made it
The order and time in which each part must be made
Each part's name, quantity, size and material
The price the customer must pay for the gate

questions.stem: Which type of drawing shows where the sockets, switches and lights are placed in the rooms of a building?
options: A circuit (schematic) diagram
A layout drawing (floor plan)
A wiring diagram of a panel
A block diagram of the supply

questions.stem: On an electrical layout plan, how do you find out what each symbol means?
options: Guess from the shape and size of each symbol
Ask the customer who owns the building
Read the dimension lines near each symbol
Check the key (legend) on the drawing

questions.stem: What does a circuit (schematic) diagram mainly show?
options: The exact position of each cable in the walls
The size and shape of each room in the house
How the parts of a circuit connect to work
The cost of each item used in the circuit

questions.stem: On a fabrication drawing, how is a welding symbol linked to the joint it refers to?
options: By an arrow line pointing to the joint
By a dashed hidden line round the joint
By a chain line drawn through the joint
By a note written in the title block

questions.stem: In a welding symbol, what does a small triangle on the reference line mean?
options: A butt weld
A fillet weld
A spot weld
A plug weld

questions.stem: Which is the best choice for making a neat freehand sketch?
options: A felt marker on plain card
A ballpoint pen on scrap paper
Chalk on a piece of steel plate
A pencil on squared (grid) paper

questions.stem: Why should a sketch be drawn roughly in proportion?
options: So that it can be measured with a rule
So that it can be used instead of a quotation
So that it looks like a computer drawing
So that the shape is easy to understand

questions.stem: Devon sketches a steel window grill for a house in Mandeville. What must he add so that the workshop can make it?
options: A drawing of the whole house around the window
All sizes, the material and the number needed
A coloured picture of a finished grill
The name of the person who will weld it

questions.stem: You must sketch an existing object. What should you do first?
options: Study it and decide which views are needed
Measure the overall length and leave the other sizes
Draw a large title block in ink across the page
Photograph it and then put the object away

questions.stem: Which tool is best for measuring the outside diameter of a small round bar for a sketch?
options: A tape measure
A try square
A vernier caliper
A protractor

questions.stem: What is the first thing to do when you are given a drawing for a new job?
options: Read the title block and the notes
Start cutting the largest part
Fold it small to fit in your pocket
Measure the drawing with a rule

questions.stem: How should paper drawings be looked after in a workshop or on site?
options: Folded small and kept in a back pocket
Pinned on the wall beside the welding booth
Left on the bench so that everyone can use them
Kept clean and dry, in a folder or holder

questions.stem: Two sizes on a drawing do not add up to the overall length shown. What should you do?
options: Use whichever size looks right to you and carry on
Stop and ask the supervisor or the person who drew it
Change the overall length on the drawing so it matches
Make the part anyway and hope that it fits

questions.stem: What is the size of an A4 sheet of paper?
An electrical drawing shows a socket outlet at "300 mm AFFL". What does AFFL mean?
options: Above floor, from the left
Above finished floor level
Along the front face line
At the far floor line

questions.stem: Which view shows the true shape of the front face of a part?
options: Plan
End elevation
Isometric view
Front elevation

questions.stem: A customer sends you a phone photo of a hand sketch for a job. What should you check before using it?
options: That the photo was taken in colour
That the photo file is small enough to send on
That all the sizes are clear and confirmed
That the sketch was drawn in pen, not pencil

questions.stem: You notice a mistake on a drawing that the whole team is using. What is the right action?
options: Tell the supervisor so it can be put right
Correct your own copy in pen and tell nobody else
Ignore it, because drawings are always right
Throw the drawing away and work from memory instead

questions.stem: In a welding symbol, what does a small circle at the bend between the arrow line and the reference line mean?
options: Weld on site
Weld all round
Grind the weld flat
Spot weld only

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A drawing says "4 holes at 50 CRS". What does CRS stand for?
What does the abbreviation THK mean on a drawing?
A material note on a drawing says "MS flat bar". What does MS stand for?
A drawing shows one hole with the note "TYP" beside it. What word does TYP stand for?
A small part is drawn at a scale of 2:1. A line on the drawing is 30 mm long. What is the real length in millimetres?
A length on a sketch is written as 2.4 m. What is this length in millimetres?
What is the name of the thin line drawn out from the edge of a part to show where a dimension starts or ends?
What is the name of the drawing that shows how all the parts of a product fit together?
What is the name of the drawing of one single part that shows all of its sizes?
The projection symbol on a drawing shows two views of which solid shape?
Name the drawing instrument with a point and a pencil, used to draw circles and arcs on paper.
Name the flat, triangle-shaped drawing tool used to draw lines at 30°, 60° and 90°.
Name the electrical drawing that shows how each wire is connected to the terminals of the equipment.
Three hole centres are in a straight row, 40 mm apart. How far is the first hole centre from the third, in millimetres?
What do we call a quick drawing made by hand, without drawing instruments?

essays.stem: Describe what you should read and check on a drawing before you start work on a job.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the title block. I check the drawing title and number to make sure it is the right job, and the revision letter and date to make sure it is the latest copy. I check the scale, and the projection symbol so that I know whether it is first or third angle and where each view is. I check the units, which are usually millimetres, and any general tolerances. Then I read the notes and the parts list, which tell me the material, the thickness or size, the finish and how many of each part are needed. I look at each view to understand the shape, including hidden lines and sections. If any size is missing, unclear or does not add up, I ask my supervisor before I start.
markingPoints: Title, drawing number, revision and date checked
Scale and projection symbol checked
Units and tolerances checked
Notes and parts list read for material, finish and quantity
Asks the supervisor about anything missing or unclear

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would make a dimensioned freehand sketch of an existing steel bracket or an empty metal electrical box.
essays.modelAnswer: First I look at the object carefully and decide which views I need, usually a front view, a plan and an end view, and sometimes an isometric view as well. I use a pencil and squared paper. I draw light construction boxes for each view, roughly in proportion and lined up with each other, then draw the outlines more firmly. I add centre lines for holes and dashed lines for hidden edges. Next I measure the object with a tape, steel rule or vernier caliper, and write the sizes on the sketch with dimension lines and arrows, all in millimetres. I add notes for the material, the thickness, the hole sizes and the number needed. I finish with a title, my name, the date and "NTS" (not to scale). Last, I check the sketch against the object to be sure no size is missing.
markingPoints: Studies the object and chooses the views needed
Pencil and grid paper; light boxes in proportion, views lined up
Measures with suitable tools and adds dimensions in mm
Adds notes: material, thickness, holes, quantity; title, name, date, NTS
Checks the sketch against the object for missing sizes

essays.stem: Compare an isometric sketch with an orthographic drawing. Say when you would use each one.
essays.modelAnswer: An isometric sketch shows the object in three dimensions in one picture. The upright edges are drawn vertical and the other edges are drawn at 30° to the horizontal. It is easy for anyone, including a customer, to understand the shape at a glance, so it is useful for showing an idea, explaining a job or showing how parts fit together. However, round holes look like ovals, hidden details are hard to show, and it is not good for showing every size. An orthographic drawing shows the object as two or more flat views, such as front, plan and end views, each seen straight on. Each view shows true shapes and sizes, so all dimensions, holes and hidden details can be shown clearly. It is used as the working drawing to make the part in the workshop or on site.
markingPoints: Isometric: one 3D view, edges at 30°, easy to understand
Isometric: good for ideas, customers and assembly; poor for full sizes and hidden detail
Orthographic: two or more flat views seen straight on
Orthographic: true shapes and full dimensions; used as the working drawing

essays.stem: Explain what a drawing scale is, and how you would choose a scale to draw a large steel gate and a small electrical fitting on an A4 sheet.
essays.modelAnswer: A scale tells you how the size on the drawing compares with the real size. At 1:1 the drawing is full size. A reduction scale such as 1:10 makes the drawing ten times smaller than the real object, and an enlargement scale such as 2:1 makes it twice as big. A steel gate might be 3 m wide, which is far too big for an A4 sheet that is only 297 mm long, so I would choose a reduction scale such as 1:20, which makes it 150 mm wide and leaves room for the views, dimensions and title block. A small electrical fitting, for example a 20 mm wide clip, would be too small to show clearly at 1:1, so I would use an enlargement scale such as 2:1. Whatever scale I use, I write it in the title block and write the real sizes on the dimensions.
markingPoints: Explains a scale as the ratio of drawing size to real size
Gives reduction and enlargement examples correctly
Chooses a reduction scale for the gate so it fits with room for dimensions
Chooses full size or an enlargement for the small fitting
States the scale in the title block and writes real sizes on the dimensions

essays.stem: Describe the good practice for putting dimensions on a sketch or drawing so that it is clear and cannot be misread.
essays.modelAnswer: Each size should be shown once only, so that two sizes cannot disagree. I use thin extension lines that start a small gap away from the outline, and thin dimension lines with clear arrowheads that touch the extension lines. The numbers are written clearly above the dimension line, so that they can be read from the bottom or right of the sheet. I give sizes in millimetres and write a note to say so. Where possible I measure from one datum edge, so that errors do not build up. I do not use outline or centre lines as dimension lines. I show the overall length, width and height, and give hole sizes as diameters with their positions to the centres. Any tolerance is written beside the size. Finally I check that someone else could make the part from my sizes alone.
markingPoints: Each size shown once only
Thin extension and dimension lines with clear arrowheads and readable numbers
Units stated and sizes taken from a datum
Overall sizes, hole diameters and positions to centres given
Tolerances shown and the drawing checked for completeness

essays.stem: Explain how you would use a building layout plan (floor plan) to plan work in a room, for example fixing sockets and lights or fitting steel burglar bars to the windows.
essays.modelAnswer: I first check the title block for the scale, the revision and the room names, so that I am in the right room with the latest plan. I read the key or legend to understand each symbol, such as sockets, switches, lights, doors and windows. I use the scale and the written sizes to find the positions and the distances between items, and I check any heights given, such as above finished floor level. I count the items to work out how many fittings, boxes, lengths of steel or bars I need, and I note the window sizes or cable routes. Then I visit the room and check the real sizes against the plan, because walls and windows are not always built exactly as drawn. I mark any differences on my copy and tell my supervisor before ordering materials or starting work.
markingPoints: Checks the title block: scale, revision, room
Uses the key or legend to read the symbols
Uses sizes and scale to find positions, distances and heights
Counts items and works out the materials needed
Checks the plan against the real room and reports differences

essays.stem: Explain why drawings must be kept up to date and controlled in a workshop, and what can go wrong if an old drawing is used.
essays.modelAnswer: Drawings change when a customer asks for something different, when a mistake is found or when a better way is chosen. Each change is given a new revision letter or number and a date, so that everyone can see which copy is the latest. Old copies should be removed or clearly marked as old, so that nobody uses them by mistake. If a worker uses an old drawing, the parts may be the wrong size, holes may be in the wrong place or the wrong material may be used. The job may not fit on site, so time and material are wasted and the job must be done again. This costs the business money and can upset the customer. In electrical work a wrong drawing could also mean the wrong circuit is wired, which is unsafe. That is why I always check the revision before starting.
markingPoints: Drawings change, and each change gets a new revision and date
Old copies are removed or marked so that only the latest is used
Using an old drawing gives wrong sizes, holes or materials
Results: rework, waste, cost, delay and an unhappy customer, or unsafe work
Workers check the revision before starting

essays.stem: Describe how you would read a drawing of a welded steel frame to make a cutting list of its parts.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the title block and the revision first, then read the notes and the parts list for the material, such as 25 mm square tube or 40 mm × 5 mm flat bar. I look at each view to understand how the frame is put together and which parts meet at each corner. For each part I find its length on the drawing, taking care to see whether the corners are mitred or butted, because that changes the cut length. I write the cutting list as a table, with the part mark, the description, the section size, the length and the number needed. I add up the total length of each section so that I can see how many stock lengths are needed. Last, I check the list against the drawing again and ask my supervisor to look at it before any material is cut.
markingPoints: Checks the title block, revision, notes and parts list
Studies the views to understand how the parts fit and the corner joints
Finds the correct cut length of each part
Sets out the cutting list as a table: part, section, length, quantity
Totals lengths for ordering and checks the list before cutting

essays.stem: Describe what you would do if a drawing is unclear, has a missing size, or does not match what you find on site.
essays.modelAnswer: I would not guess. First I read the drawing again carefully, including the notes, the other views and any other drawings for the same job, because the size may be shown somewhere else. I check that I have the latest revision. If the problem is still there, I stop work on that part and tell my supervisor, showing exactly where the problem is. If the site does not match, for example a window is a different size or a wall is in a different place, I measure the real size carefully, take a photo and make a sketch with the sizes. The supervisor or the person who made the drawing can then decide what to do and give a corrected drawing or a written instruction. I write down what was agreed, with the date, and keep it with the job papers.
markingPoints: Does not guess; re-reads the drawing, the other views and the notes
Checks for the latest revision
Stops and reports to the supervisor or the person who drew it
On site, measures, photographs and sketches the real situation
Gets a corrected drawing or written instruction and records it

essays.stem: Explain how centre lines, hidden detail lines and sectional views help you understand a part that has holes and hollow spaces inside it.
essays.modelAnswer: Centre lines are thin chain lines drawn through the middle of holes, round parts and anything that is the same on both sides. They show where the centre of each hole is, so I can mark it out and drill it in the right place, and sizes are often given to the centre lines. Hidden detail lines are thin dashed lines. They show edges and holes that are behind the surface and cannot be seen in that view, such as a hole going right through a block or a slot on the back. A sectional view shows the part as if it has been cut through, with the cut surface hatched with thin lines at 45°. This makes the inside clear, without lots of confusing dashed lines, so I can see wall thickness, the depth of holes and the shape of hollow parts.
markingPoints: Centre lines: thin chain lines through the centres of holes and round parts
Centre lines help in marking out and measuring to centres
Hidden detail: thin dashed lines for edges that cannot be seen
Sections: part shown cut through, with hatching on the cut surface
Sections make inside shapes, depths and thicknesses clear

practical1.title: Measure and sketch a workshop item in orthographic and isometric views
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group one real item to sketch, such as a small welded steel bracket or an empty metal electrical box that is not connected to anything. As a group, study the item and agree which views are needed and which projection you will use. Every member measures part of the item with the correct tool and records the sizes. Each member then draws at least one part of the finished sheet in pencil on grid paper: the front view, the plan, the end view, the isometric sketch, or the title block and notes. Put the views together on one A3 sheet (or join A4 sheets), lined up correctly, with all dimensions in millimetres, the material, the number needed, the projection used, your names, the date and "NTS". Finish by checking the sketch against the item together. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: One workshop item per group (a small steel bracket or an empty metal box)
Steel rules, a 5 m tape measure and a vernier caliper
Grid paper (A4 and A3) and plain paper
A clipboard or drawing board for each member
photos: The item on the bench, with the group agreeing the views
Members measuring the item with the rule, tape and vernier caliper
The page of measured sizes written down
Each member's view or part of the sheet in progress
The finished sheet with all views, dimensions and the title block
The group checking the sketch against the item
checklist: Took part in choosing the views and the projection
Used the right measuring tool correctly and wrote sizes clearly in mm
Drew their view in proportion, with firm outlines and light construction lines
Used the right line types: outlines, hidden lines and centre lines
Lined up the views correctly for the projection chosen
Added dimensions that are clear, shown once and complete
Completed the notes and title block (material, quantity, projection, names, date, NTS)
Checked the finished sketch against the item and corrected any mistake
safety: Use only an item the assessor has given you; never sketch an electrical box that is connected
Watch for sharp edges and burrs on the item; wear gloves to handle it if needed
Close the vernier caliper jaws and put tools away after use
Keep the bench clear and do not leave tools where they can fall

practical2.title: Read a drawing and build a full-size card model of a sheet-metal part
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a simple drawing of a sheet-metal part, such as an open tray, a cover plate with a folded flange, or a small bracket with holes. As a group, read the drawing and fill in the interpretation sheet: the title, drawing number, revision, scale, projection, material, thickness, overall sizes, hole sizes and positions, and the number needed. Then mark out the flat shape of the part full size on card, with cut lines drawn solid and fold lines drawn as chain lines, and cut, fold and tape it into a model. Share the work so that every member fills in part of the sheet, marks out part of the shape, and checks at least two sizes on the finished model against the drawing. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with the interpretation sheet.
materials: The drawing of the sheet-metal part and an interpretation sheet
Steel rules, set squares, compasses and pencils
Craft knives with retractable blades and a cutting mat
Scissors, masking tape or glue stick
photos: The group reading the drawing, with the interpretation sheet partly filled in
The flat shape marked out full size on card, with cut and fold lines
The shape cut out and ready to fold
The finished card model beside the drawing
A steel rule on the model checking a size, and the area cleaned up
checklist: Read the title block correctly (title, number, revision, scale, projection)
Read the sizes, holes and notes correctly on the interpretation sheet
Worked out full-size measurements correctly from the drawing
Marked out accurately, with cut lines and fold lines drawn differently
Cut and folded safely and neatly
Model sizes match the drawing within the tolerance set by the assessor
Explained one feature of the drawing to the assessor in their own words
safety: Cut on the cutting mat, away from your body and hands, using a steel rule as a guide
Retract the knife blade every time you put the knife down
Pass knives and scissors handle first
Put used blades and offcuts in the correct bin
